extracted.intended_audience: students, general readers, and aspiring writers or critics studying E. M. Forster's life and fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze E. M. Forster's life, themes, techniques and critical reception to inform literary analysis or to model aspects of novel/short-story writing in the Forsterian tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanist characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: "The humanist has four leading characteristics – curiosity, a free mind, belief in good taste, and belief in the human race." (Forster's humanist attitude is at the heart of his work.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster's fiction and essays express a humanist outlook; evaluate works by how well they manifest curiosity, intellectual openness, aesthetic judgment ('good taste'), and faith in human dignity and connection. See his essay 'What I Believe' for the articulation of this stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of personal connections despite social restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster 'often depicts the pursuit of personal connections despite the restrictions of contemporary society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plots and character arcs by whether they foreground attempts at human connection constrained by class, propriety, empire, or sexual norms (a central motive across his novels and stories). Examples: A Room with a View, Howards End, A Passage to India.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of class differences and irreconcilability
rubrics_metrics.description: Two of Forster's best-known works, A Passage to India and Howards End, 'explore the irreconcilability of class differences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scenes and social realism by how they dramatize class divisions, tensions between social groups, and whether the narrative treats reconciliation or intractability convincingly. Howards End (Schlegels, Wilcoxes, Basts) is an explicit model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Forster is noted for his use of symbolism as a technique in his novels."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and evaluate recurring symbols (e.g., the wych elm in Howards End; mystical links between characters such as Mrs Wilcox and Mrs Moore). Consider whether symbolism enriches theme without becoming obscure or merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of diverse national characters and cosmopolitanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster (with Henry James and W. Somerset Maugham) was among the earliest English writers to portray characters from diverse countries — France, Germany, Italy and India — exploring cultural conflict while foregrounding humanism and cosmopolitanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural representation for nuance and complexity: does the work portray cross-cultural encounter and conflict thoughtfully, avoiding reductive stereotyping while examining power imbalances (as in A Passage to India)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and depiction of sexuality (including homosexuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster's works (notably Maurice and some short stories) explore sexuality and homosexuality; Maurice was written earlier but published posthumously and was controversial. Forster also publicly advocated legal change regarding homosexuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or modeling writing on sexuality, consider frankness, historical context, and the relationship between personal identity and social constraints. Note critical debates about the influence of Forster's sexuality on his fiction and the controversies around publishing such material in his era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believability of romantic/sexual pairings
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical reception has included comments on 'unlikely pairings of characters who marry or get engaged and the lack of realistic depiction of sexual attraction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative criterion, check whether romantic outcomes are earned by character development and credible sexual/psychological attraction; avoid implausible pairings that strain readers' suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with social and political critique; prescient/dystopian insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster's short story 'The Machine Stops' (1909) is 'often viewed as the beginning of technological dystopian fiction' and is praised for vivid engagement with real-world social and political issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speculative or socially critical writing by its clarity of social diagnosis, scope of critique, and prescience — does it illuminate present-day issues through compelling speculative detail (as critics note in comparisons with We and Brave New World)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition-of-England / social-ambition novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Howards End is described as an ambitious 'condition-of-England' novel about various groups among the Edwardian middle classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large-scale social fiction, assess how effectively the novel uses representative families/groups to dramatize broader social conditions and historical change. Look for balance between social panorama and individual characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mysticism (as technique or motif)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forster 'has been criticised ... for his attachment to mysticism.' Examples include mystical links between characters that suggest connection beyond social circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mystical elements as a stylistic choice: evaluate whether they enhance the novel's moral or thematic aims, or whether they appear ungrounded. Critics cite mysticism as both a strength (evoking depth) and a vulnerability (risk of vagueness).
